implementation_notes: Scala's default form is a plain class or trait: declare trait Mediator { def notify(sender: Colleague, event: Event): Unit }, implement the coordination in a class that keeps colleagues in a mutable collection, and let participants hold the mediator as a constructor parameter. Traits give the abstraction without a framework, case classes give a closed and pattern-matchable event vocabulary, and matching in the mediator replaces the classic notify-then-if - the GoF structure with less ceremony and no subclassing of participants. Keep it for synchronous, local coordination; when the hub must own state concurrently, the typed-actor variant is the Scala ecosystem's answer.
pitfalls: A mutable buffer of colleagues is not thread-safe; a hub shared across threads needs an immutable snapshot plus @volatile/synchronized, or an actor (see the sibling variant).
Case-class events are a closed set: adding one is a compile-time reminder in every match, but wildcard cases that swallow unknown events hide protocol drift.
Colleagues held strongly by the hub keep each other alive; remove participants or hold them weakly when the mediator outlives them.

variants.name: Typed actor hub (Apache Pekko)
variants.idiom_name: ActorRef[Event] + Behavior with one message at a time (Pekko typed)
variants.implementation_notes: In the Scala ecosystem the mediator is often an actor: the hub is a typed actor whose Behavior[Event] owns the coordination state, participants hold only an ActorRef[Event] and send with tell/!, and the runtime guarantees one message is processed at a time - no locks, and a state change is simply the next behavior returned for the message. Pekko's typed API (pekko-actor-typed) makes the protocol explicit: ActorRef[T] is the address, tell has at-most-once semantics, and behaviors are built with Behaviors.receive. Use it when the collaboration is concurrent, long-lived or distributed; keep the plain trait mediator for in-thread coordination, since an actor system is a large dependency.
pitfalls: tell/! is fire-and-forget with at-most-once semantics: there is no reply unless the protocol carries a replyTo ActorRef, and a lost message is lost.
An actor processes one message at a time, so a blocking operation inside the behavior stalls the hub and occupies a dispatcher thread; use a dedicated dispatcher or async pipeTo.
Actor state is not shared: colleagues must not keep mutable references across messages, so model changes as the next Behavior rather than fields mutated from outside.
A Behaviors.receive that does not match a message drops it into dead letters; match the full protocol or handle unknown messages explicitly.
